# Appendix H — Anti-Pattern Catalog

This catalog lists the anti-patterns described in the Common Pitfall callouts of each chapter, so that a review can scan them in one place. Each entry names the problem; the section it links to explains the consequences and what to do instead.

## H.1 Chapter 1: Architecture Requirements

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Writing functional requirements as interface descriptions — “the system shall display an order summary page.” | 1.1 |
| Optimizing one attribute locally and declaring victory. | 1.2 |
| Recording a team preference as a constraint. | 1.3 |
| Accepting “highly available” as a requirement. | 1.4 |
| Building the traceability matrix once, at design time, and then treating it as complete. | 1.5 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 1

## H.2 Chapter 2: Architecture Principles

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Publishing principles as adjectives — “secure”, “scalable”, “cloud-first” — with no rationale or guardrail. | 2.1 |
| Building a capability map once, for a funding deck, and never updating it. | 2.2 |
| Choosing a service per team because the organization chart changed. | 2.3 |
| A “common” library that every module edits becomes a shared release dependency, and the boundaries disappear while the deployment diagram still shows separate boxes. | 2.4 |
| Declaring “the data warehouse is read-only” while analysts correct records there and the corrections are loaded back into production. | 2.5 |
| Calling a protocol choice a contract: “we use REST, so it is decoupled”. | 2.6 |
| Authorizing only in the user interface or the gateway. | 2.7 |
| Adding retries to fix a flaky dependency without a deadline or an idempotency key. | 2.8 |
| Extrapolating capacity from instance count or from average latency. | 2.9 |
| Instrumenting infrastructure and calling it observability: CPU dashboards for every host, no business transaction that can be followed end to end. | 2.10 |
| Letting a vendor SDK shape the domain model because it was quickest at the start. | 2.11 |
| Reuse enforced through a shared release train: every team adopts the shared component, and every team now releases together. | 2.12 |
| Recording only the outcome of a decision, not the alternatives or the assumption that made it correct. | 2.13 |
| Logging full request payloads for debugging convenience. | 2.14 |
| Naming a team as the owner and keeping the evidence only in chat history. | 2.15 |
| Publishing “prefer asynchronous integration” without an exception route. | 2.16 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 2

## H.3 Chapter 3: Architecture Decisions

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Deciding significance by novelty — recording the unfamiliar technology and skipping the boring decision. | 3.1 |
| Recording a constraint as a decision. | 3.2 |
| Treating microservices, or any pattern, as a maturity level. | 3.3 |
| An ADR that reads like meeting minutes: attendees, discussion and a conclusion, with no alternatives, no consequences and no trigger. | 3.4 |
| Keeping traceability in a spreadsheet that a project manager updates by hand. | 3.5 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 3

## H.4 Chapter 4: Architecture Governance

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Publishing a governance model that names forums but not decisions. | 4.1 |
| Deciding by consensus because no owner was named. | 4.2 |
| Shipping a guardrail without a violation fixture. | 4.3 |
| Reviewing every change or approving none. | 4.4 |
| Renewing the same waiver each quarter without remediating it. | 4.5 |
| Storing documents in team folders with no identifiers. | 4.6 |
| Making a noisy check blocking. | 4.7 |
| Counting meetings, documents and approvals as evidence of governance. | 4.8 |
| Collecting screenshots in the two weeks before an audit. | 4.9 |
| Reorganizing teams around a new architecture diagram without moving ownership of the running system. | 4.10 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 4

## H.5 Chapter 5: Data Architecture

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Publishing principles as aspirations — "data is an asset", "we are data-driven" — with no owner, control or exception process. | 5.1 |
| Treating the analytical copy as the convenient source of truth: a dashboard queries the warehouse because it is faster, then a business decision depends on data that is hours old, lacks a correction path and never receives deletions. | 5.2 |
| Confusing schema validity with trust: a contract test passes, so the data is assumed correct, while units, nullability or survivorship silently changed. | 5.3 |
| Applying one consistency level to the whole estate — usually the strongest available — because "correctness matters". | 5.4 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 5

## H.6 Chapter 6: Integration Architecture

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Choosing asynchronous messaging to "decouple" without designing the pending state the user will see. | 6.1 |
| Treating the OpenAPI document as the whole contract. | 6.2 |
| Treating a broker’s at-least-once delivery as end-to-end exactly-once. | 6.3 |
| Converting every timeout into a failure. | 6.4 |
| Monitoring the broker and calling it integration reliability. | 6.5 |
| Letting the integration layer become the application. | 6.6 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 6

## H.7 Chapter 7: Application Architecture

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Choosing microservices before the boundaries and ownership are understood. | 7.1 |
| Letting adapters decide business outcomes: a provider client that maps a timeout to "declined", or a controller that sets an order to REJECTED when validation fails. | 7.2 |
| Adding a projection or a cache to solve a performance problem that is actually a query or index problem. | 7.3 |
| Adding retries and instances to a system whose bottleneck is a shared resource. | 7.4 |
| Publishing a shared library that contains domain logic — an `order-utils` package with pricing rules and state transitions — because it avoids duplicating a few functions. | 7.5 |
| Letting a BFF become a second domain layer. | 7.6 |
| Relying on an application-level tenant filter as the only isolation control. | 7.7 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 7

## H.8 Chapter 8: Infrastructure and Cloud Architecture

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Treating "managed" as "secured". | 8.1 |
| A second region is provisioned, but DNS, identity, secrets and operational access are not replicated, so the first failover test fails at the first step and the region turns out to be a diagram rather than a recovery capability. | 8.2 |
| Optimizing the invoice line that looks largest instead of the unit economics. | 8.3 |
| Building a platform nobody asked to use: capabilities chosen by the platform team, delivered through a ticket queue, with no adoption measure. | 8.4 |
| Closing framework findings by editing the questionnaire answer. | 8.5 |
| Testing connectivity from an administrator workstation or a jump host and concluding the workload can reach the dependency. | 8.6 |
| Adopting a container orchestrator as a default for a small number of services. | 8.7 |
| Designing the fleet as if devices were always connected and always current. | 8.8 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 8

## H.9 Chapter 9: Security Architecture

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Running threat modeling once at design time and filing the result. | 9.1 |
| Treating a valid OAuth access token as proof of user identity. | 9.2 |
| Relying on a role check at the API gateway. | 9.3 |
| Encrypting data and treating key custody as an implementation detail. | 9.4 |
| Relying on an unauthenticated DAST scan as the security test. | 9.5 |
| Prioritizing only by CVSS base score. | 9.6 |
| Treating operational logs as an audit trail. | 9.7 |
| Accepting a certification logo without reading its scope and period. | 9.8 |
| Treating pseudonymized data as anonymous. | 9.9 |
| Assuming TLS and an API gateway are sufficient. | 9.10 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 9

## H.10 Chapter 10: Observability, Reliability and SRE

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Collecting everything and controlling nothing. | 10.1 |
| Setting the SLO equal to the SLA, or at 100%. | 10.2 |
| Setting severity from the technical cause instead of customer impact. | 10.3 |
| Sizing for the average and trusting autoscaling to cover the peak. | 10.4 |
| Treating the postmortem as the end of the incident: the document is filed, the actions have no owner or date, and the team moves to the next release. | 10.5 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 10

## H.11 Chapter 11: Deployment and Operations

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Building a different artifact for each environment. | 11.1 |
| Keeping every flag forever. | 11.2 |
| Treating go-live as a deployment milestone. | 11.3 |
| Using the emergency route to hit a deadline. | 11.4 |
| Standing break-glass access. | 11.5 |
| Assuming every release can be rolled back. | 11.6 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 11

## H.12 Chapter 12: Architecture Documentation

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Documenting every view the notation allows. | 12.1 |
| Drawing the success path and calling the dynamic view done. | 12.2 |
| Treating documentation as a phase deliverable. | 12.3 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 12

## H.13 Chapter 13: Architecture Evaluation

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Treating a reviewed diagram or an approval meeting as validation. | 13.1 |
| Turning the evaluation into design by committee. | 13.2 |
| Treating the evaluation report as the end of the work. | 13.3 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 13

## H.14 Chapter 14: Testing and Quality Verification

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Optimizing for a coverage number instead of for evidence. | 14.1 |
| Re-running the pipeline until it turns green. | 14.2 |
| Testing quality attributes once, before the first launch. | 14.3 |
| Turning test metrics into targets for teams. | 14.4 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 14

## H.15 Chapter 15: Architecture Evolution and Economics

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Treating a migration plan as a schedule rather than a risk-reduction sequence. | 15.1 |
| Comparing options on the number that is easiest to obtain. | 15.2 |
| A migration that never retires old paths is accumulation, not modernization. | 15.3 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 15

## H.16 Chapter 16: Software Engineering and Architecture Artifacts

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Producing every artifact for every change. | 16.1 |
| Treating the PRD as the requirements baseline and leaving quality attributes to the architect. | 16.2 |
| Writing the ADR after the work is done, as a summary that justifies what was built. | 16.3 |
| Maintaining the ICD as prose while the OpenAPI file evolves independently. | 16.4 |
| Treating approval as the end of an artifact’s life. | 16.5 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 16

## H.17 Chapter 17: Architecture Frameworks, Methods and Standards

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Positioning frameworks by reputation rather than by concern. | 17.1 |
| Using an enterprise framework to document a single solution. | 17.2 |
| Running an evaluation method as a ratification ritual. | 17.3 |
| Citing a regulation by name in a design document without confirming applicability or the current edition. | 17.4 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 17

## H.18 Chapter 18: AI and Machine Learning Architecture

| Anti-pattern | Section |
| :--- | :--- |
| Reviewing an AI design as if the model were the system. | 18.1 |
| Starting with the most capable pattern. | 18.2 |
| Indexing everything and filtering at answer time. | 18.3 |
| Selecting a model from a public leaderboard or a single impressive demo. | 18.4 |
| Treating the system prompt as the security boundary. | 18.5 |
| Shipping prompt and index changes as configuration rather than as releases. | 18.6 |
| Optimizing the invoice line that is easiest to see. | 18.7 |
| Giving an agent a service account with the combined permissions of everyone it serves. | 18.8 |

: Anti-patterns from Chapter 18
